study_identification_part.si4_title: Extreme deviations from the normative model reveal cortical heterogeneity and associations with negative symptom severity in first-episode psychosis from the OPTiMiSE and GAP studies

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To apply normative modelling to investigate heterogeneity in cortical thickness in first-episode psychosis with three aims: (1) quantify cortical thickness heterogeneity by mapping regional cortical thickness deviations at the individual level, (2) assess group-level differences in deviations from the expected pattern of cortical thickness between patients and control participants, and (3) evaluate the relationship between cortical thickness deviations and symptom severity (PANSS), treatment response and clinical outcome both at baseline and over the medium term (0-95 weeks, median timepoints = 4).

The underlying neurobiological pattern is highly heterogeneous, with extreme negative deviations detected in almost all brain regions and no more than 6.4% of patients displaying extreme deviations in the same region (compared to 5.4% in controls). FEP patients displayed a higher percentage of extreme negative deviations across the 148 atlas regions (1.77%) than control participants (0.77%), and controls displayed higher percentage of extreme positive deviations (0.88%) than patients (0.59%). Mann-Whitney U tests revealed significantly lower z-scores in FEP patients across multiple regions in frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p<0.05). Longitudinal LME models showed that negative symptoms improved over time (coefficient=-0.116, p=4×10⁻⁶) and that thinner cortex at baseline predicted more severe negative symptoms (coefficient=-0.154, p=0.001). Twelve specific regions remained significant after multiple comparison correction, including left postcentral gyrus (coef=-0.198, p<0.001), left inferior parietal gyrus (coef=-0.176, p<0.001), left superior occipital gyrus (coef=-0.167, p<0.001), right superior temporal gyrus (coef=-0.144, p<0.01), and left superior temporal gyrus (coef=-0.146, p<0.01). Regional cortical deviations did not significantly predict positive or general PANSS scores. For remission status, left central gyral deviations showed significant association (coef=0.415, odds ratio=1.423, p=0.0004) with thinner cortex predicting lower likelihood of remission."}

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a well-designed study applying state-of-the-art normative modeling to first-episode psychosis. Key strengths include: (1) large sample size (n=295 FEP), (2) very large reference normative model (n=37,126 across 79 scanners), (3) rigorous handling of site effects through hierarchical Bayesian regression with federated learning, (4) longitudinal clinical follow-up (median 4 timepoints, up to 95 weeks), and (5) careful model adaptation procedure. The study makes important contributions by demonstrating extreme heterogeneity even at first episode, and by showing that individual-level cortical deviations have predictive value for negative symptoms where traditional case-control approaches failed. The GAP sample was supplemented with ATLAS data (n=124 controls) to ensure adequate representation of older age range for model adaptation. The study performed sensitivity analyses excluding sites with <10 controls, showing robust results. Notable limitation is the lack of validation on completely independent external cohorts from different studies/scanners.
